actions.justification: Mandatory first step: Patient has CKD stage 4 and is scheduled for cardiac catheterization with contrast. Hydration status is critical to assess CI-AKI risk and guide pre-procedure hydration strategy.
Mandatory: CKD stage 4 patient requires baseline eGFR to quantify renal function, determine contrast volume limits, and risk-stratify for contrast-induced nephropathy before catheterization.
Mandatory: Patient has multiple CI-AKI risk factors (CKD stage 4, diabetes). Comprehensive risk factor review guides pre-procedural optimization and nephroprotective strategies.
Establish current baseline vitals prior to contrast administration, given CKD stage 4 and diabetes which increase CI-AKI risk.
Review current medications for nephrotoxins (e.g., NSAIDs, metformin, ACE inhibitors) that should be held before contrast exposure in this high-risk patient.
Calculate maximum safe contrast volume based on eGFR (CKD stage 4) to minimize contrast-induced nephropathy risk during cardiac catheterization.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, placing them at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Before proceeding with cardiac catheterization using iodinated contrast, alternative imaging modalities should be considered to minimize contrast exposure risk.

CKD stage 4 with diabetes represents high risk for contrast-induced AKI. Nephrology consultation is indicated to optimize renal protection strategy, assess need for pre-procedure hydration protocol, and guide peri-procedural management.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes is at elevated baseline risk. All nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, ACE inhibitors if applicable) should be held or avoided prior to contrast administration to minimize additive renal injury risk.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and is scheduled for cardiac catheterization with contrast exposure. Documenting the eGFR check is essential to establish baseline renal function and guide contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) prevention strategy.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes is at high risk for contrast-induced AKI. Discontinuing nephrotoxic agents (e.g., NSAIDs, metformin) prior to contrast administration is a guideline-recommended preventive measure.
Baseline urine output assessment is critical in this high-risk patient (CKD stage 4, diabetes) prior to contrast exposure to guide hydration strategy and detect early signs of renal compromise.
Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes. Metformin should be held before and after contrast administration due to risk of lactic acidosis, especially with impaired renal function.

Pre-procedural IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid (normal saline or sodium bicarbonate) is a cornerstone of contrast-induced nephropathy prevention in high-risk patients with CKD stage 4 and diabetes undergoing cardiac catheterization.
Review and adjust renally-dosed medications given CKD stage 4 (eGFR likely 15-29 mL/min) to prevent drug accumulation or toxicity around the time of the procedure.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and is undergoing contrast administration. Holding nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, etc.) pre- and peri-procedurally reduces the risk of additive renal injury and contrast-induced nephropathy.

CKD stage 4 corresponds to eGFR 15-29 (G4), which exceeds the G3b threshold. Metformin must be held before and after contrast administration to prevent lactic acidosis risk in the setting of potential acute kidney injury.
Post-contrast IV hydration with isotonic saline is a cornerstone of CIN prevention in high-risk patients (CKD stage 4 + diabetes). This should be planned and initiated after the procedure.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, placing them at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN). Pre-procedural IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid is a cornerstone of CIN prevention per nephrology/cardiology guidelines. Although post-contrast hydration is already ordered, confirming pre-contrast hydration is optimized is critical before cardiac catheterization.
Continuous urine output monitoring is essential in this high-risk CKD stage 4 diabetic patient undergoing contrast exposure to detect early signs of acute kidney injury and guide hydration adequacy.

Serial serum creatinine monitoring at 48-72 hours post-contrast is the standard of care for detecting contrast-induced nephropathy in high-risk patients (CKD stage 4 + diabetes). Scheduling this now ensures follow-up is not missed.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes undergoing cardiac catheterization is at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Serial serum creatinine at 48 hours post-contrast is standard of care to detect CI-AKI early.
Ongoing optimization of fluid status is essential in a CKD stage 4 diabetic patient post-contrast exposure to protect renal function and prevent contrast-induced nephropathy.
Pre-procedural ECG is indicated for a patient undergoing cardiac catheterization to establish baseline cardiac rhythm and identify any conduction abnormalities.
